title: From Implicit, Hard-Coded Objectives to Explicit, Learned Goals

html:
Every objective described so far–viability regulation, compression progress, empowerment, attachment, belonging, status, fairness, identity coherence–is, in the first instance, implicit: it is realized not as a proposition the organism entertains but as an architectural bias–a wiring pattern, a receptor distribution, a neuromodulatory gain schedule, a genetically timed sensitive period–that shapes computation without ever being "represented" in the format that would allow the organism to inspect, verbalize, or deliberately revise it. A newborn whose separation-distress circuit fires upon loss of skin contact is not pursuing the goal "maintain proximity to caregiver"; a toddler whose dorsal striatum chunks a reach-grasp sequence is not pursuing the goal "expand my action-channel capacity"; a teenager whose ventral striatum fires to peer approval is (probably) not pursuing the goal "maximize social empowerment." These objectives are enacted by the architecture but not tokened in any workspace where they could be deliberated over, traded off against one another, or communicated to others. Yet adult humans routinely do all of these things: they set explicit goals ("finish the dissertation by June"), rank-order competing objectives ("career vs. family"), report their motivations to others ("I want to feel more in control of my life"), and adopt culturally transmitted purposes ("reduce global poverty") that bear no resemblance to anything evolution could have directly installed. How does the implicit objective stack described above give rise to the explicit, linguistically structured, culturally scaffolded goal representations that characterize human agency? This subsection traces the computational and neural bridge between the two regimes and argues that explicit goals are best understood not as replacements for implicit objectives but as learned, compressed, communicable re-descriptions of policy-relevant subproblems discovered by the implicit stack operating over a lifetime of structured experience.

A useful operational criterion: a goal is explicit to the extent that it is (i) represented in a format accessible to working memory and deliberative planning (i.e., tokened as a discrete state in prefrontal-parietal workspace circuits rather than embedded only in synaptic weights or neuromodulatory set-points), (ii) encodable in a compositional symbolic medium (paradigmatically natural language, but also imagery, diagrams, or formal notation–any medium that supports combinatorial recombination), and (iii) selectable and revisable by the agent’s own meta-cognitive control system–the agent can choose to adopt, abandon, or modify the goal in response to changing circumstances, new information, or competing objectives. On this definition, explicit goals are data structures in working memory that function as target states for model-based planning: they specify a desired region of (latent) state space, and the planning system searches for policies π*\pi^* such that Q(sτ∣π*)≈Pgoal(sτ)Q(s_\tau \mid \pi^*) \approx P_{\text{goal}}(s_\tau). Implicit objectives, by contrast, shape behavior through architectural constraints on the learning and inference process itself–they bias which policies are explored, which prediction errors are attended to, and which state transitions are reinforced, without needing to be represented as target states in any explicit planning computation. The distinction is not binary but graded: an objective can be partially explicit ("I feel restless and want to do something" registers a drive without specifying a target state) or situationally explicit (the thirsty organism may represent "find water" as an explicit subgoal while the deeper homeostatic regulation of osmolality remains implicit). In a 2025 reversal-learning study of 10–22-year-olds, performance improved with age, with the steepest gains in early adolescence (Figure) 11. Flexible reactions to negative feedback were related to reversal-learning performance, with the association most pronounced in adults (Figure).

The computational bridge: how implicit objectives generate explicit goals

The bridge from implicit to explicit proceeds through three inter-dependent mechanisms, each scaffolded by architectural priors and refined by experience:

(1) Interoceptive and affective "surfacing": implicit drives become felt states. The first step is that implicit viability constraints generate interoceptive prediction errors and affective valence signals that are accessible to cortical inference. When blood glucose drops, the hypothalamic-brainstem homeostatic controller does not merely adjust insulin and glucagon; it also generates an ascending signal that is registered by insular cortex as a felt state (hunger) and by anterior cingulate as a motivational urgency signal. This "surfacing" converts an implicit set-point deviation into a phenomenologically accessible datum–a prediction error that the agent’s generative model can attempt to explain and resolve via deliberate action. Active inference formalizes this: interoceptive prediction errors that cannot be resolved by autonomic reflexes (the "interoceptive inference" route 1) are "passed up" the hierarchy until they reach levels capable of active inference–generating actions ("go to the kitchen") rather than merely adjusting internal parameters. The felt state is thus an interface representation: it translates an architectural constraint (glucose << set-point) into a format compatible with the explicit planning machinery of prefrontal cortex. Importantly, not all implicit objectives surface equally well. Viability-level drives (hunger, thirst, pain, thermal discomfort, social distress) generate strong, identifiable felt states because their rapid resolution is fitness-critical. But subtler objectives–compression progress, empowerment, long-run social-capital maintenance–generate weaker, more diffuse affective signals (curiosity, restlessness, vague dissatisfaction, ennui) whose correct interpretation requires substantial meta-cognitive development. Much of the developmental trajectory from childhood to adulthood involves learning to read these subtler signals accurately: recognizing that the restlessness one feels is a compression-progress signal ("I need a harder challenge"), or that the vague unease in a social situation is an empowerment signal ("I have no influence here"), or that chronic low mood reflects a belonging deficit rather than a personal failing. A 2026 study examines reported bodily activation (Figure) 12. The study compares subjective activation with skin conductance (Figure).

(2) Model-based decomposition: felt needs become subgoal structures. Once an implicit drive has surfaced as a felt state, the prefrontal-hippocampal planning system can decompose it into a structured subgoal hierarchy via prospective simulation. The hungry organism does not simply emit random foraging behavior; it simulates candidate action sequences ("open the fridge →\to retrieve leftovers →\to heat them →\to eat"), evaluates each against the felt need, and selects the plan whose terminal state best resolves the interoceptive prediction error. Each node in this plan is an explicit subgoal–a target state representation maintained in working memory and monitored by ACC/frontoparietal control circuits. The decomposition process is itself a compression operation: a high-dimensional, continuous drive ("restore glucose homeostasis") is compressed into a discrete sequence of achievable waypoints, each expressible in a compact representational format. This is where the hierarchical option/skill architecture described in the Empowerment section becomes critical: the agent can only plan in terms of actions it can already execute as chunked units. A skilled cook decomposes "make dinner" into a few high-level steps; a novice must plan at a much finer grain. The available option library thus determines the resolution at which explicit goals can be formulated–another instance of empowerment constraining the effective goal space. The task design distinguishes flexible use of a learned state space (Figure) 14. The replay examples connect internal sequences with future choices (Figure) 15.

(3) Linguistic encoding: subgoals become communicable propositions. The qualitative leap from primate-level subgoal pursuit to human-level explicit goal representation is catalyzed by language. Once a subgoal can be encoded in a compositional symbolic format ("finish the dissertation by June"), it acquires properties that no purely sensorimotor goal representation possesses: A study tests reading while working-memory demands vary (Figure) 16. The study analyzes how cognitive load relates to performance (Figure).

Displacement: The goal can refer to states that are spatiotemporally remote, counterfactual, or abstract–"reduce global carbon emissions," "become the kind of person who keeps promises"–transcending the reach of sensorimotor simulation 2.

Compositional generativity: Goals can be combined, negated, conditioned, and embedded ("if the weather is good, hike; otherwise, finish chapter 3") using the same syntactic machinery that structures sentences, enabling goal structures of unbounded complexity.

Social shareability: A linguistically encoded goal can be communicated, enabling coordination ("let’s both aim for XX"), delegation ("your job is YY"), negotiation ("I’ll do XX if you do ZZ"), and cultural transmission ("our community values WW"). This transforms goal pursuit from an individual to a collective computational process, vastly expanding the effective planning horizon and resource base.

Reflective accessibility: A verbalized goal can become an object of the agent’s own meta-cognitive scrutiny ("is this really what I want?"), enabling deliberate goal revision, prioritization, and abandonment–the operations that distinguish human agency from stimulus-driven or habit-driven behavior.

The neural interface between goal representation and language is supported by the dense connectivity between prefrontal goal-maintenance circuits (especially left DLPFC and frontopolar cortex) and the perisylvian language network (left IFG, posterior temporal cortex) via dorsal and ventral white-matter pathways 3, 4. Inner speech–the covert linguistic rehearsal that accompanies much of human planning and self-regulation–may be the primary vehicle through which subgoal representations are maintained in working memory in linguistic format, leveraging the phonological loop as a goal-maintenance buffer 5, 6. Vygotsky’s observation that children progress from overt self-directed speech ("now I put the red block on top") to covert inner speech during problem-solving 7 documents the developmental moment at which linguistic encoding is internalized as a planning tool–the point at which the child gains the capacity to hold explicit, compositional, revisable goal representations in a format that can also be externalized for social coordination.

The relationship between implicit and explicit: alignment, scaffolding, and conflict

The relationship between implicit objectives and explicit goals is best characterized not as replacement but as hierarchical scaffolding with imperfect alignment. Explicit goals are generated in the service of implicit objectives–they are the plans that the organism’s deliberative system constructs to satisfy the drives that the implicit stack has surfaced–but the mapping is neither one-to-one nor guaranteed to be faithful. Several systematic patterns of alignment and misalignment are worth distinguishing: The homeostatic state-space model makes physiological reward explicit (Figure) 13.

Faithful instrumentality. In the simplest case, explicit goals are accurate instrumental decompositions of implicit drives: "drink water" faithfully serves hydration homeostasis; "practice the piano piece" faithfully serves compression progress in the musical domain; "apologize to my friend" faithfully serves attachment/belonging maintenance. Here the explicit goal is a well-calibrated proxy for the implicit objective, and pursuit of the explicit goal reliably reduces the implicit drive. Most everyday goal-directed behavior falls in this regime–the implicit-to-explicit translation is straightforward because the agent’s world model is accurate, the relevant drive has surfaced clearly, and the available options are well-matched to the problem.

Approximate proxies and Goodhart drift. More commonly, explicit goals are approximate compressions of implicit objectives that sacrifice fidelity for tractability. "Get a high GPA" is a learnable, measurable proxy for the deeper objectives of compression progress (learning), social empowerment (career options), and belonging (meeting parental expectations), but it can diverge from all three: a student who optimizes GPA by memorizing rather than understanding sacrifices compression; one who chooses easy courses over challenging ones sacrifices empowerment (skill expansion); one who cheats risks social exclusion if discovered. This is the social-cognitive analogue of Goodhart’s Law 8: once a proxy is adopted as an explicit target, the optimization process can exploit the gap between proxy and true objective 9. In the brain, such divergence manifests as a conflict between explicit goal pursuit and implicit affective signals: the student who is "succeeding" by GPA metrics but not learning may experience persistent dissatisfaction, boredom, or anxiety–interoceptive/affective prediction errors from the compression and empowerment drives signaling that the explicit goal is not resolving the underlying implicit need. Whether the agent heeds these signals depends on meta-cognitive capacity (can it recognize the source of the discomfort?) and on the relative precision weighting of explicit goal-monitoring circuits vs. implicit affective feedback–a balance that is itself developmentally and contextually modulated.

Culturally transmitted goals with no direct biological grounding. Human explicit goals frequently have no straightforward mapping to any single implicit objective. "Prove Fermat’s Last Theorem," "achieve enlightenment," "write the great American novel," "end factory farming"–these are goals whose content is specified by cultural models rather than biological drives, and whose pursuit may require sustained effort against multiple implicit drives (physical discomfort, social isolation, opportunity cost to empowerment in other domains). Yet they are pursued with an intensity and commitment that rivals or exceeds biologically grounded drives. Two complementary mechanisms explain this:

Goal adoption via social-identity integration. As described in "Theories of Minds", the self-model includes group memberships and cultural role commitments as core identity components. When an agent identifies as a "mathematician," "Buddhist," "novelist," or "animal rights activist," the goals associated with that identity enter P(π∣θi)P(\pi \mid \theta^i)–the prior over policies conditional on the self-model–and deviation from them generates identity-threat distress (cognitive dissonance, shame). The implicit belonging and identity-coherence drives thus provide motivational fuel for culturally specified goals that would otherwise lack biological grounding. The goal is "explicit" in content but is powered by implicit drives that care not about the specific content but about maintaining coherence between behavior and self-model. Learned intrinsic value via compression/empowerment bootstrapping. A domain that initially offers high compression progress (mathematics is deeply compressible; artistic creation generates high ΔL\Delta L) or high empowerment gain (mastering a complex skill dramatically expands the action-outcome channel) can become intrinsically valued through standard value-learning: dopaminergic RPEs reinforce the states and policies associated with the domain, and over time the domain itself–with all its culturally specific goal structures–acquires cached value that persists even when the marginal compression/empowerment returns diminish. This is the mechanism by which the implicit drive for learning progress "hands off" to an explicit, culturally structured goal: the initial engagement is driven by rtintr^{\text{int}}_t; the sustained commitment is maintained by learned value, social identity, and the sunk-cost dynamics of expertise investment. From the outside, the mature expert pursuing a culturally defined goal looks like an agent with a "terminal value" for that goal; from the inside, it is the endpoint of a developmental trajectory in which implicit drives discovered, engaged with, and ultimately delegated sustained motivation to, a learned objective. The study applies its classifiers to social feedback (Figure) 17.

Explicit goals that conflict with implicit objectives (akrasia, self-destructive goal pursuit, ideological override). The most consequential misalignment arises when explicit goals actively oppose implicit drives. Classic akrasia (weakness of will)–eating the cake despite the explicit goal of dieting–reflects a failure of prefrontal goal maintenance to override subcortical/habitual policy selection when the implicit drive (caloric homeostasis in an energy-scarce-adapted system) and the explicit goal (long-run health in an energy-abundant environment) point in opposite directions. The converse pattern, where explicit goals override implicit welfare signals, is equally important and often more consequential: religious ascetics suppress hunger, sexual desire, and comfort drives in pursuit of identity-congruent spiritual goals; political ideologues sacrifice personal safety and social bonds for abstract causes; perfectionists pursue explicit achievement targets well past the point where compression and empowerment drives have saturated, driven by identity-threat/shame avoidance rather than positive learning progress. In these cases, the explicit goal has captured the motivational system by engaging the identity-coherence and belonging drives at high precision while suppressing or overriding the affective signals from other implicit objectives. The capacity for such override is a distinctively human feature–enabled by the prefrontal control architecture’s ability to maintain abstract goal representations with sufficient precision to dominate subcortical valuation–and it is simultaneously the source of humanity’s greatest achievements (sustained pursuit of goals requiring decades of effort against biological drives) and its most spectacular pathologies (ideological fanaticism, self-destructive perfectionism, addiction to culturally defined status metrics).

Cultural amplification: how explicit goals transcend individual biology

The capacity for explicit, linguistically encoded, socially shared goals is the mechanism by which human motivation escapes the bounds of individual biology. Three features of cultural goal systems merit emphasis:

Goal inheritance and cumulative refinement. Culturally transmitted goals can persist across generations, accumulating refinements that no single individual could achieve. The goal "understand the fundamental laws of physics" has been pursued across centuries by successive communities of scientists, each inheriting the compressed models (theories) and explicit subgoal structures (open problems) of predecessors. This is inter-generational compression progress: each generation’s contribution is a ΔL\Delta L that reduces the description length of physical phenomena, but the accumulated L0−LTL_0 - L_T over generations dwarfs anything achievable within a single lifespan. Cultural institutions (universities, journals, professional societies) function as external memory and coordination infrastructure that maintains explicit goal structures, accumulated knowledge, and quality-control norms across the temporal horizon that biological memory cannot span.

Institutional goal structures. Human societies construct institutional goals–the objectives of organizations, governments, religions, and social movements–that are super-individual: they are pursued by collectives of agents, persist beyond any individual’s lifespan, and can coordinate behavior at scales (millions of agents, decades of time) that no individual goal representation could. Institutional goals are "explicit" in an extended sense: they are encoded in constitutions, mission statements, legal codes, and strategic plans–external representations that function as shared priors over policy space for all members of the institution. Individual agents adopt institutional goals via the social-identity mechanism described above: identifying as a member of institution II imports II’s goals into one’s own policy priors, powered by belonging and identity-coherence drives. The result is a multi-scale goal hierarchy: individual implicit drives →\to individual explicit goals →\to group/institutional goals →\to civilizational aspirations, with each level scaffolded by the one below and enabled by the cultural technologies (language, writing, institutions) that support goal representation and coordination at that scale.

Normative goal structures and moral progress. Cultural goal systems include not only instrumental objectives ("build a bridge") but normative ones ("create a just society"). As described in "Theories of Minds", the norm-learning architecture installs sensitivity to fairness, harm, and reciprocity, but the scope of these norms is culturally specified. The historical expansion of moral concern–from kin to tribe to nation to (in some modern frameworks) all sentient beings 10–can be understood as a culturally driven expansion of the set of entities included in P(oτ)P(o_\tau)’s preference distribution: each expansion redefines "preferred outcomes" to include welfare states of a larger circle, generating new explicit goals (abolish slavery, extend suffrage, reduce animal suffering) that would have been unrepresentable in earlier cultural contexts. These goals are "explicit" in the strongest sense: they require compositional linguistic encoding, abstract moral reasoning, and institutional coordination to pursue, and they often conflict with implicit drives (in-group favoritism, status competition, resource hoarding) whose architectural biases must be deliberately overridden. A 2025 study catalogs everyday moral dilemmas (Figure) 18. A 2026 study presents professional ethical dilemmas to university students (Figure) 19.

Synthesis: the full objective stack

The full picture of human motivation is therefore a multi-layered objective stack in which each layer emerged through a different mechanism, operates on a different timescale, and is represented in a different neural format:

Layer Origin Neural format Timescale of change
Viability constraints (homeostasis, pain) Phylogenetic (genetic specification of set-points & alarm circuits) Brainstem/hypothalamic set-points; interoceptive prediction error Evolutionary (10510^5-10610^6 years)
Implicit learning drives (compression, empowerment) Phylogenetic architecture + ontogenetic meta-learning Neuromodulatory gain schedules; intrinsic reward signals; architectural biases (sparse coding, hierarchical prediction) Architectural: evolutionary; tuning: developmental (10010^0-10110^1 years)
Implicit social objectives (attachment, belonging, status, fairness) Phylogenetic architecture + sensitive-period calibration Neuropeptide/neuromodulatory circuits (OT, opioid, 5-HT); social-pain/reward overlap; IWMs Architectural: evolutionary; calibration: infancy-adolescence
Explicit personal goals Ontogenetic: model-based decomposition of implicit drives PFC working-memory representations; hippocampal-PFC prospective simulation; linguistic encoding Minutes to years (adopted, revised, abandoned within lifespan)
Identity-level commitments Ontogenetic + cultural: self-model integration of roles, values, group memberships CMS (mPFC/PCC) self-model; DMN consolidation; identity-affect circuits Years to decades (high-inertia learned priors, revisable under strong evidence)
Cultural/institutional goals Cultural transmission via language, narrative, institutions External representations (texts, laws, norms) internalized via social-identity mechanisms Generations to centuries (cumulative cultural evolution)

These layers do not operate in isolation but form a coupled dynamical system. Implicit drives generate the felt states that motivate explicit goal formation; explicit goals, once adopted, reshape the training distribution for implicit learning (a student who explicitly commits to studying physics exposes their compression drive to physics-structured data, biasing future intrinsic motivation toward that domain). Identity commitments constrain explicit goal selection (goals inconsistent with identity are filtered before deliberation); cultural goal systems shape the identities available for adoption (one cannot identify as a "scientist" in a culture without science). Upward causation (implicit →\to explicit) and downward causation (cultural →\to identity →\to explicit →\to implicit training distribution) operate simultaneously, producing a co-constructive dynamic in which no single layer has absolute priority.

The question "what objective does the human brain optimize?" now has a layered answer:

At the architectural level (fixed within a lifetime): minimize long-run variational free energy, subject to viability constraints–which decomposes into risk minimization (preference satisfaction), ambiguity reduction (state estimation), and model improvement (compression progress), with empowerment as the option-value prior and social objectives as deep viability-level priors on the preference landscape.

At the meta-learning level (tuned across development): the implicit stack’s operation over structured experience generates a meta-learned exploration/exploitation policy (see "Intrinsic Motivation") that implicitly approximates: "allocate resources to domains and experiences where model improvement, skill expansion, and social capital accumulation are jointly maximized per unit cost."

At the explicit goal level (revised within episodes to years): the agent pursues a portfolio of linguistically structured, culturally informed, identity-constrained goals that are best understood as locally optimal compressions of the implicit stack’s demands given the agent’s current world model, option library, social context, and identity commitments. These explicit goals are the "conscious objectives" that the agent would report if asked "what are you trying to do?"–but they are shadows cast by a much deeper, wider, and older objective structure that operates largely below reflective awareness.

The practical consequence is that human behavior cannot be predicted or understood from explicit goals alone, because explicit goals are (a) incomplete compressions of the full implicit stack, (b) subject to Goodhart drift under optimization pressure, (c) in chronic low-grade tension with implicit drives that surface as affect, and (d) embedded in a social/cultural context that shapes which goals are available, valued, and identity-consistent. Equally, behavior cannot be predicted from implicit drives alone, because the explicit goal layer–enabled by prefrontal control, language, and cultural scaffolding–can sustain behavioral programs that override, redirect, and even counteract implicit drives for extended periods. Understanding human motivation requires modeling the full stack and its interactions: the ancient implicit objectives that generate the energy for action, the learned explicit goals that give it direction, and the cultural institutions that extend both scope and horizon far beyond anything a solitary biological optimizer could achieve.
